lessons.title: Volcker's Disinflation: How the Fed Broke the Back of Inflation in the Early 1980s

children.text: In the early 1980s, homebuilders mailed pieces of two-by-four lumber to the US Federal Reserve, a protest against mortgage rates that had made building or buying a house unaffordable. Farmers drove tractors to Washington. Auto dealers mailed in car keys they could no longer sell against loans at those rates. All of this anger was aimed at one man: Paul Volcker, the Fed Chair who had decided that the only way out of the wage-price spiral from the last lesson was to deliberately cause a recession large enough to break it.

body.text: Volcker's disinflation proved something uncomfortable: breaking an entrenched inflation regime rarely needs a clever new tool. It needs a central bank willing to accept a large, real, politically painful recession, and to refuse to blink until inflation expectations actually break. Credibility is not free.

events.title: Volcker Sworn In
events.description: President Carter appoints Paul Volcker as Fed Chair specifically to fight the inflation that had run through most of the decade, inheriting the fully entrenched wage-price spiral from the previous lesson.

events.title: The "Saturday Night Special"
events.description: In an unscheduled Saturday announcement, the Fed shifts its operating target from the federal funds rate to the growth rate of bank reserves, a monetarist approach that lets interest rates rise however high was needed to slow money and credit growth.

events.title: The First Recession
events.description: The federal funds rate spikes and the US economy tips into a brief recession within months, before the Fed eases slightly, only for inflation to remain elevated.

events.title: The Second, Deeper Recession
events.description: The Fed tightens again, and the federal funds rate approaches 20% at its peak. Unemployment climbs through 1982, eventually peaking near 10.8% in November-December 1982, the highest US unemployment rate since the Great Depression at that point.

events.title: Inflation Finally Breaks
events.description: US CPI inflation falls to roughly 3.2%, down from a peak above 13% just three years earlier. President Reagan, despite the recession's political cost, reappoints Volcker in 1983, backing the policy through to its conclusion.

children.text: The Saturday Night Special: Targeting Money, Not Rates

Until October 1979, the Fed had mostly managed the economy by setting a target for the federal funds rate directly, adjusting it gradually and trying to avoid shocking markets or voters. Volcker's shift, influenced by monetarist economics, was to instead target the growth rate of bank reserves and let the interest rate go wherever it needed to go to hit that target. This mattered because it took political blame off the Fed's hands for any single rate decision, the rate was now a consequence of the reserves target, not a discretionary choice, while still delivering the same outcome: interest rates high enough to genuinely choke off credit growth and, with it, the demand and wage-price dynamics that had kept inflation running for a decade.

The Homebuilder's View
body.scenario: A homebuilder in 1981 can no longer sell new houses. Mortgage rates linked to the Fed's tightening have crossed the high teens, so almost no buyer can afford the monthly payment on a new home loan, even though the homebuilder's own costs have not particularly changed.
body.prompt: From the homebuilder's perspective, this policy looks like an unnecessary disaster caused entirely by the Fed. From Volcker's perspective, this pain was the mechanism, not a side effect. Explain why a policymaker would accept, and even require, this level of damage to defeat an inflation regime like the one from the last lesson.
body.modelAnswer: By 1979, the US economy's wage-price spiral was running partly on expectations: workers demanded higher wages because they expected prices to keep rising, and businesses raised prices because they expected costs to keep rising, regardless of what current demand actually justified. A moderate rate hike would not break that expectation, because everyone had already lived through a decade of moderate hikes followed by the Fed backing off once growth slowed. Only a shock severe enough to visibly crush demand, and to convince households and businesses that the Fed would keep rates high even through a painful recession, could break the self-fulfilling expectation that inflation would keep running. The homebuilder's pain was not incidental; it was the visible proof that the Fed's commitment was real, which is exactly what made the disinflation credible and, ultimately, lasting.

body.text: This was not a popular policy in real time. Volcker faced sustained political attacks, protests outside the Fed, and calls for his removal, at a moment when unemployment was the highest it had been since the Great Depression. It only reads as an obvious success in hindsight, once the inflation had actually broken and stayed broken for decades afterward.

children.text: Why the Pain Was the Point: Central Bank Credibility

Volcker's disinflation is the founding case study for what economists now call central bank credibility. Once markets, businesses, and workers genuinely believed the Fed would tolerate a severe recession rather than let inflation re-accelerate, inflation expectations fell faster than the underlying economic data alone would predict, because expectations themselves are a real input into future inflation. The decades that followed, often called the Great Moderation, saw much lower and steadier inflation across major economies, not because the world stopped experiencing oil shocks or demand booms, but because central banks had established that they would respond forcefully rather than accommodate. The global spillover was real too: the sudden spike in dollar interest rates helped trigger the 1982 Latin American debt crisis, as countries that had borrowed heavily in dollars found their debt service costs exploding overnight. India, still a largely closed, capital-controlled economy in 1979-83, was mostly insulated from this specific shock, a form of protection that came with its own costs, which the next chapter takes up directly.

columns.label: Burns' Fed, 1970s
points: Treated inflation as an external, cost-push problem beyond the Fed's control
Kept rates relatively low to avoid recession and political backlash
Allowed inflation expectations to drift upward and become self-fulfilling
Result: a decade of entrenched, recurring inflation

columns.label: Volcker's Fed, 1979-83
points: Treated inflation as ultimately a monetary regime the Fed was responsible for
Accepted a severe, deliberately engineered recession to break it
Held the line through intense political pressure until credibility was established
Result: inflation broken within about three years, and low for decades after

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why did Volcker's October 1979 shift to targeting bank reserve growth, rather than the interest rate directly, matter for the credibility of the disinflation?
options: It allowed the Fed to keep interest rates permanently low
It let the interest rate rise as a consequence of a monetary target, rather than as a discretionary Fed choice, and it removed the earlier pattern of backing off once growth slowed
It transferred control of monetary policy from the Fed to the US Treasury
It eliminated the need for any recession at all
body.explanation: The mechanism itself was less important than the commitment it signalled: by targeting reserves and letting rates go wherever needed, the Fed showed it would not simply ease off once the pain became politically uncomfortable, which is exactly what had undermined credibility through the 1970s.

points: Volcker's Fed broke the 1970s wage-price spiral by accepting a severe, deliberately engineered recession, not by finding a painless technical fix.
The October 1979 shift to targeting bank reserve growth let interest rates rise as far as needed, and signalled a break from the Fed's earlier pattern of backing off under political pressure.
The federal funds rate approached 20% and unemployment peaked near 10.8% in late 1982, the direct, real cost of the disinflation.
US CPI inflation fell from roughly 13.5% in 1980 to about 3.2% by 1983, and stayed low for decades, an outcome credited largely to restored central bank credibility.
India, still a closed and capital-controlled economy at the time, was largely insulated from this specific global shock, insulation that came with its own tradeoffs, the subject of the next chapter.
